newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Midday Update.

text.p: GOVERNMENT COMMITTEE DISAPPOINTED BY STEEL CLOSURE
The head of the Federal Government's bi-partisan Steel Industry advisory committee, Victorian MP, David Hawker, says the decision by BHP to close steelmaking operations in Newcastle is regrettable.
Unions estimate the closure, confirmed by BHP this morning, will cost two-and-a-half thousand jobs.
Mr Hawker says the committee is most disappointed to see further job losses flowing from the decision.
Secretary of Newcastle's Trades Hall Council, Peter Barrack, says he's extremely disappointed that the time frame for the closure has been brought forward two years to 1999.
JAPAN OPENS DOOR TO AUSSIE RICE
Japan has further opened its highly-protected rice market to allow some Australian rice sales.
At the conclusion of leaders talks in Canberra, the Prime Minister, John Howard, said Japan would change its schedule to give Australia the chance to sell seven-thousand tonnes of new season rice.
Mr Howard said he accepted Mr Hashimoto's idea of annual summits between the two leaders and he looked forward to visiting Japan next year.
The Japanese Prime Minister will fly to New Zealand this afternoon.
OPPOSITION CALLS PM'S WIK PLAN A LANDGRAB
The Shadow Minister for Aboriginal Affairs, Daryl Melham, says the Prime Minister has been conned by pastoralists, because they can upgrade their leases to freehold title at taxpayers' expense.
Mr Howard has announced he'll draft legislation as soon as possible to expand pastoral rights and limit native title rights in response to the High Court's Wik decision.
Mr Melham says that amounts to a landgrab of monumental proportions.
Aboriginal leaders are meeting in Canberra today and tomorrow to prepare their formal response to the Prime Minister's plan.
INDIGENOUS LEADERS WORKING ON RESPONSE TO 10-POINT-PLAN
Aboriginal leaders say they remain opposed to any moves to diminish the rights of Indigenous people to negotiate over the use of pastoral land where native title exists.

The National Indigenous Working Group, charged with negotiating with the Government on the Wik issue, is meeting in Canberra to prepare a response to the Prime Minister's 10-point-plan on native title.
The group says it's also opposed to any plan which extinguishes native title ineffect, even if not in legislation.
The government will soon draft legislation to expand the rights of pastoralists and limit the right of Aborigines to negotiate over land use.

National Party President Don McDonald says he understands John Howard's plan allows pastoralists to upgrade their leases to freehold title, and provides for compensation to Aborigines if native title is proven.
He says his party won't accept the plan unless that's the case.
HANSON RELEASES FIRST POLICY
Federal MP Pauline Hanson has told industry to forget the waffle from other parties and look at a new deal from her One Nation party.
Ms Hanson has released her party's first policy... consultation.
She says she wants to talk with small business, building, manufacturing, mining, taxation and farming representatives, because it's only from these groups that real long term jobs will be created.
Ms Hanson says the new deal she's offering is a fair deal for all Australians, who've had enough of seeing policies re-arranged for political reasons.
FISCHER BACKS HOWARD PLAN ON WIK
Deputy Prime Minister, Tim Fischer, says he's batting for the Prime Minister's ten-point plan on Native Title because freeholding land sand-bags it against high court challenges.
Queensland's United Graziers Association says the proposal doesn't go far enough and continues to push for legislation to extinguish Native Title.
Mr Fischer has told ABC Radio the ten point plan is not set in concrete and he too is committed to ensure pastoral leaseholders have certainty.
He says one of the problems with extinguishment is that it can still be open to future High Court action.
IRISH MUM'S PLAN TO SUE QLD GOVERNMENT
A woman in Ireland is planning to sue the Queensland Government after a police bungle led to a three week delay in her being told her daughter had died in a diving accident off the Whitsundays.
Sheila Lynch from County Cavan in Ireland, died while snorkelling at Hardy Reef last month.
Police say a communication breakdown led to her body remaining in the Mackay morgue for almost three weeks -- before the family found out about the tragedy while making their own inquiries.
Mother, Kathlene Lynch, says the police handling of the matter was shocking and has devastated her family.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
